1.0.0.en: Tribute: taxes that an occupied people pay to the one who enslaves them.

1.0.1.en: The prophet marvels at the destruction that has come upon Jerusalem and likens her to a great lady who has become a sorrowful widow, rejected by others. After Jerusalem was a great city full of inhabitants, she has now become a ruin, and the weak Jews who remain in her are enslaved to Babylon and pay tribute.

1.0.2.en: When a person forsakes God, Satan humiliates him, so he withdraws from all the believers, feels lonely, and devotes his strength to evil. Consider the consequences of sin so that you may keep away from it, and do not let its pleasures allure you, for they are deceptive and temporary, hiding behind them humiliation and torment.

1.1.0.en: He portrays the isolation of Jerusalem as a widow weeping alone in the night, when all who were allied with her are asleep. All have abandoned her, and she sits in sorrow, weeping over the destruction that has come upon her. This is a symbol of the human soul that sits in the darkness of sin, suffering its consequences and grieving over all that has befallen it after all those who encouraged it to do evil have abandoned it.

1.2.0.en: He explains the state of Jerusalem, taken captive by Babylon, as follows:

1.2.1.en: 1- She became enslaved to Babylon and humiliated.

1.2.2.en: 2- The loss of peace and rest, while the nations around her rejoice and enjoy themselves.

1.2.3.en: 3- She could not flee and be saved from the Babylonian siege; rather, the armies of Babylon were able to enter the city, destroy it and burn it, so the people were in great distress.

1.3.0.en: Zion: what is meant is Jerusalem, for it is her ancient name.

1.3.1.en: He continues explaining the state of humiliated Jerusalem as follows:

1.3.2.en: 1- Jerusalem was deprived of keeping the feasts of the Lord, because she had been destroyed and the Jews no longer came from all the lands to Jerusalem to keep the feast.

1.3.3.en: 2- The gates of Jerusalem were broken and burned, that is, she lost her security and protection.

1.3.4.en: 3- The priests who lead the worship in the temple of Jerusalem were in deep sorrow, because the temple had been burned and they could not offer the sacrifices and serve God.

1.3.5.en: 4- The sorrow of her virgins, meaning the bitterness of all the souls in her, since they weep over the ruin of their great city.

1.3.6.en: [2] Sin is the cause of humiliation (vv. 5-9)

1.3.7.en: 5- Her adversaries are the chief, her enemies prosper; for the LORD hath afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions: her children are gone into captivity before the enemy. 6- And from the daughter of Zion all her beauty is departed: her princes are become like harts that find no pasture, and they are gone without strength before the pursuer. 7- Jerusalem remembered in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that she had in the days of old, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy, and none did help her: the adversaries saw her, and did laugh at her destruction. 8- Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is become an abomination: all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yea, she sigheth, and turneth backward. 9- Her filthiness is in her skirts; she remembereth not her last end; therefore she came down wonderfully: she had no comforter. O LORD, behold my affliction: for the enemy hath magnified himself.

1.4.0.en: The enemies of Jerusalem grew great and ruled over her like chiefs, while she was in humiliation, because the Lord Himself permitted this as discipline for her sins, whether because of the worship of idols or evil lusts. The enemy seized the best of her sons and took them to Babylon as slaves.

1.4.1.en: Sin makes a person lose his strength. So remember, my brother, that you are the image of God and a temple of His Holy Spirit, so live for Him and do not defile yourself with sin; thus you keep your strength and rejoice with God.

1.5.0.en: Harts: a kind of deer that moves swiftly.

1.5.1.en: Because of the evils of Jerusalem, she lost all her greatness and beauty and her chiefs who led her and managed her affairs, for they were in great fear before the enemy and fled swiftly, as harts run far away in search of food when they find no pasture to eat in. For Jerusalem was in hunger and those in her were about to die, so the king and the chiefs made a breach in the wall of the city and fled from it. But the enemy's armies seized them and killed them, and humiliated the rest of them, who became extremely weak, and Babylon took them captive. The armies of Babylon pursued everyone who tried to flee and seized him.

1.6.0.en: During the destruction of Jerusalem she remembered her worldly lusts and the evils in which she had been immersed, and saw that she had lost all her pleasures. He portrays Jerusalem as a woman staggering from weakness and fear before the enemy, and in her humiliation the Babylonian enemies mocked her, corrupted her and destroyed her.

1.7.1.en: Her nakedness: he likens Jerusalem to a woman who came into shame after being stripped of her garments, that is, she became a ruin with no glory in her.

1.7.2.en: He makes clear that the humiliation and contempt that came upon Jerusalem are because of her sin. All the neighbors of Jerusalem who used to honor her despised her while she was in shame, for there was no longer in her the temple or palaces, but the stinking corpses of the slain, and the rest of her sons had fled from her or been taken by the enemy into captivity.

1.8.0.en: He likens Jerusalem to an adulterous woman whose skirts reveal her uncleanness and her fall into evil, that is, the cause of Jerusalem's destruction is her fall into unclean lusts. Sadly, when Jerusalem was immersed in uncleanness she forgot that she was a daughter of God and did not prepare for her eternal life. Therefore, when the wrath of God came upon her, she found no one to comfort her in her sorrow, because it is God who comforts and supports His children; if they forsake Him they will find no one to comfort them and make them glad, but will be in deep sorrow.

1.8.1.en: But the prophet returns to God on behalf of Jerusalem and asks for His mercies, and that He remove from him the Babylonian enemy who has become proud and humiliated the people of God.

1.8.3.en: 10- The adversary hath spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things: for she hath seen that the heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command that they should not enter into thy congregation. 11- All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul: see, O LORD, and consider; for I am become vile.

1.9.0.en: Her sanctuary: the temple of the Lord.

1.9.1.en: The sorrow of Jerusalem was great because of the enemy's control over the whole city, but the most important thing in her is the temple of the Lord, which no pagan person may enter. Now, however, the Babylonians entered it, defiled it and burned it, after stealing the precious possessions in it.

1.10.0.en: When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, the food inside ran out and hunger grew severe among the people, and they tried to buy bread by offering the dearest things they had, that they might live. Then Jerusalem sighs in sorrow and asks for God's help because of the humiliation into which she has fallen.

1.10.1.en: The devil tries to deprive you of the bread of life, that is, Christ our God, and besieges you with sin so that you may go away from God. So do not yield to him, but hold fast to your God and remain in His Church, nourished by her Holy Sacraments and His satisfying word.

1.10.3.en: 12- Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow, which is done unto me, wherewith the LORD hath afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger. 13- From above hath he sent fire into my bones, and it prevaileth against them: he hath spread a net for my feet, he hath turned me back: he hath made me desolate and faint all the day. 14- The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand: they are wreathed, and come up upon my neck: he hath made my strength to fall, the Lord hath delivered me into their hands, from whom I am not able to rise up. 15- The Lord hath trodden under foot all my mighty men in the midst of me: he hath called an assembly against me to crush my young men: the Lord hath trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah, as in a winepress. 16- For these things I weep; mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me: my children are desolate, because the enemy prevailed.

1.11.0.en: He likens Jerusalem to a woman looking at those who pass by on the roads leading to her, while she is in ruins and sorrowful over her destruction. She calls to the passers-by to see how great her sorrow is, because God permitted her humiliation on the day of Babylon's attack upon her.

1.12.0.en: Jerusalem continues speaking to the passers-by and tells them that God sent fire and it burned her bones. She is like a woman who has been shattered, since the Babylonians burned the temple of God and the palaces of Jerusalem. Her fall into the hand of Babylon is likened to Babylon spreading a net into which Jerusalem fell as prey, and Babylon seized her; whoever could flee from Jerusalem fled, and whoever remained in her was left in perpetual humiliation and sorrow.

1.13.0.en: Yoke: a piece of wood placed on the necks of two animals to pull agricultural implements, and it is tied to the animal's neck by a wreathed rope, that is, a strong one.

1.13.1.en: Jerusalem also likens herself to an animal on whose neck the yoke has been placed, then God brought a wreathed rope and tied her neck to the yoke with it. He means that she has become enslaved to Babylon in weakness and humiliation and has lost her strength, since she fell into strong hands, the hands of Babylon.

1.14.0.en: Jerusalem declares that it is God who permits these disciplines. It is He who permitted all her strong sons, who were able to fight, to be despised, so they became weak, and her young men, that is, her strength, were crushed, because youth is distinguished by strength. Jerusalem likens herself to a virgin who has been put in a winepress, so her blood flowed and all her strength was lost.

1.15.0.en: The comforter that should relieve my soul: what is meant is God, who is able to comfort me and restore my soul to me so that I may live. What increased Jerusalem's sorrow most is her knowing that the discipline is from God, who used to comfort her and give her life in the midst of tribulations, whereas now it is He who permitted the tribulations to discipline her, and He will not comfort her because of her evil. And whenever Jerusalem looked at her slain children, their corpses lying in the streets, and at the cruelty of the Babylonian enemy, her tears flowed.

1.15.1.en: Accept God's discipline and hasten to repentance, for He is merciful and ready to remove His wrath if you return to Him. Do not despair if the tribulations increase, for He is able to remove them from you however hard the circumstances may be.

1.15.3.en: 17- Zion spreadeth forth her hands, and there is none to comfort her: the LORD hath commanded concerning Jacob, that his adversaries should be round about him: Jerusalem is become unclean among them. 18- The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment: hear, I pray you, all people, and behold my sorrow: my virgins and my young men are gone into captivity. 19- I called for my lovers, but they deceived me: my priests and mine elders gave up the ghost in the city, while they sought their meat to relieve their souls.

1.16.0.en: The prophet Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a weak woman stretching out her hands, asking for help in the face of the Babylonian attack, but sadly she found no one to help her, because God commanded that she be disciplined, so all her allies, whether Egypt or all the lands around her, abandoned her. Thus the Babylonian siege remained around Jerusalem, then the Babylonian army entered, defiled the temple and ruined all Jerusalem.

1.17.0.en: Jerusalem confesses her sins and her disobedience to God, who caused this ruin, and Jerusalem looks in sorrow as she sees her young men and youths taken as slaves into captivity with no one to help her. She calls to the nations around her, but no one moves to support her and rescue her from the hand of Babylon.

1.18.0.en: Jerusalem declares with regret that all her allies who loved her and promised to help her have abandoned her, and more than this, that the priests and the elders sought to save themselves and left the people to perish at the hand of Babylon. The priests and the chiefs tried to flee from Jerusalem, but the enemy seized them.

1.18.1.en: Do not trust in the arm of flesh, for men are not reliable and their promises are false; but trust in God, for He will save you however great the danger, and His promises are true forever.

1.18.3.en: 20- Behold, O LORD; for I am in distress: my bowels are troubled; mine heart is turned within me; for I have grievously rebelled: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death. 21- They have heard that I sigh: there is none to comfort me: all mine enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that thou hast done it: thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me. 22- Let all their wickedness come before thee; and do unto them, as thou hast done unto me for all my transgressions: for my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.

1.19.0.en: As death: those who remain in the house are in terror and fear, like the dead.

1.19.1.en: Bereaveth: it kills the young men, so their mothers are left without children, that is, bereaved.

1.19.2.en: Jerusalem cries out, and her heart boils with emotion over her slain and the humiliation into which she has come. She likens herself to a woman whose heart is violently moved and troubled within her for her young men, whose corpses lie in the streets, so Jerusalem became like a bereaved mother, and those who remained in the houses of Jerusalem became like the dead from fear.

1.20.0.en: Jerusalem says that when the nations around her heard of her trouble, no one helped her; rather, they gloated over her and rejoiced at her ruin. But she trusts that God will punish these wicked ones who gloat over her.

1.21.0.en: Jerusalem cries out to God to take vengeance on her neighbors who gloat over her, and, as He disciplined her with destruction, to punish them also. Jerusalem says this out of the abundance of her sorrow, which has left her unaware.

1.21.1.en: Cry out to God in all your tribulations and trust that He loves you; He disciplines you for a time so that you may return to Him and obtain His mercies.

1.21.2.en: The wrath of God upon Jerusalem

2.0.0.en: When Babylon attacked Jerusalem and destroyed everything in her, it deprived her of life. This is likened to the darkness that settled upon her, because of the darkness of her sin, since darkness is a symbol of sin and its evil effects. The prophet marvels in sorrow at Jerusalem's loss of all her glory and pride, which was the temple of God. Jerusalem was called the city of God among the peoples, and he calls it the footstool of God, that is, His place on earth, because in the eyes of men He dwells in heaven, as He is exalted above their thoughts; but His dwelling on earth is in His temple in Jerusalem, which was fulfilled by His Incarnation and His dwelling in His Church in the New Testament. Jerusalem was exalted by her faith and her worship of God, but she was cast down from heaven to earth when she worshiped idols and walked in her evil lusts, so she lost her pride and Babylon destroyed her.

2.1.0.en: Long ago God promised Jacob, the father of the fathers who dwelt in tents, blessing and good, but his offspring, that is, Jerusalem and Judea, walked in evil, so God swallowed up their dwellings, which are their tents, by the hand of Babylon; that is, God destroyed their dwellings so that they no longer existed, as a beast swallows its prey so that it no longer exists. He speaks of their dwellings as tents to remind them that they are strangers in the world, and that their hearts should be set on heaven and not on earthly lusts. Therefore, when they immersed themselves in lusts they lost their place and their city was destroyed.

2.1.1.en: Jerusalem relied on her walls and fortresses to protect her and did not trust in God, and she lived in her sins; therefore He destroyed her material strength, that is, her strongholds. By saying Judah he means the whole kingdom of Judah, that is, Jerusalem and Judea. The destruction was violent, so the palaces were leveled to the ground, and God permitted the Babylonians to defile the temple by entering it, and by entering the palaces of the chiefs and destroying everything.

2.2.1.en: The horn represents strength in an animal, with which it attacks other animals. Here the strength of Israel is likened to strong horns, but God broke them when He was angry with her by means of Babylon.

2.2.2.en: The right hand represents strength. God abandoned His people by drawing back His right hand, and He left Babylon to crush His people as discipline for them, that they might repent.

2.2.3.en: He also likens God's power that disciplines His people to the fire that burns His people, and this is what happened when Babylon burned the temple of God and the palaces of Jerusalem.

2.3.0.en: Tabernacle: the inner part of the tent, which is not visible to those around it.

2.3.1.en: God likens Himself to a warrior who holds the bow and shoots arrows at His people as discipline for them. Thus God appeared as an enemy to His people while disciplining them by the hand of Babylon, but He is the loving Father who wants their repentance and their return to Him. God set His right hand, that is, His power, against His people, as though He hated them, and this through the armies of Babylon, whereas in truth He wants, by His discipline, their return to Him.

2.3.2.en: And everything Jerusalem possessed and kept in her palaces of what is pleasant to man, God destroyed and slew, whether people or their possessions and treasures that they had hidden in their houses.

2.3.3.en: God's wrath appeared like that of one enraged at another, and like a mighty one pouring out fire, so Jerusalem burned. All this was accomplished by the hand of Babylon.

2.4.0.en: By God's rising up as an enemy against His people and destroying the palaces and fortresses of His city Jerusalem, her sorrow became great.

2.4.1.en: Know that your sin is a defiance of God that deserves death, and God is long-suffering toward you so that you may repent. So do not persist in evil, lest the wrath of God come upon you, but hasten to repentance to obtain His mercies, and know that He, as a Father, seeks your salvation, even through tribulations.

2.4.3.en: 6- And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle, as if it were of a garden: he hath destroyed his places of the assembly: the LORD hath caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and hath despised in the indignation of his anger the king and the priest. 7- The Lord hath cast off his altar, he hath abhorred his sanctuary, he hath given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they have made a noise in the house of the LORD, as in the day of a solemn feast.

2.5.0.en: Here he speaks of God's rejection of His people's worship of Him, by removing His tent of meeting with them, which became the temple of Solomon, which was in great Jerusalem, which he calls a garden because of her glory. God destroyed the Jews who used to gather for worship in His temple, and thus God despised the feasts of the Jews, which they call solemn feasts, among them the Sabbath day, because His people had become sin; and God did not honor even the chiefs, such as the king and the priest, because they were corrupt and led the people astray.

2.6.0.en: By burning the temple and destroying Jerusalem, God declared His rejection of the sacrifices of the Jews and of everything they consecrate to Him. More than this, He permitted the enemies to tear down the walls and humiliate the people, and so the cries of the Jews rose as in the feasts and solemn feasts, but here they were cries of sorrow instead of the voices of joy in the feasts.

2.6.1.en: Do not persist in some sin and neglect it, lest God reject your prayers and your worship. It is better for you to repent, so that your prayers become deeper and more acceptable to God.

2.6.3.en: 8- The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together. 9- Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD. 10- The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, and keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground. 11- Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city. 12- They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom.

2.6.4.en: 13- What thing shall I take to witness for thee? what thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee? 14- Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment.

2.7.0.en: Line: a string that the builder uses to make sure the wall is straight and does not lean.

2.7.1.en: Rampart: walls built to defend the city.

2.7.2.en: In God's wrath against Jerusalem He wanted to remove protection from her by tearing down her walls. Here the line is used figuratively, for the line is used to keep the building true, and God sets right Jerusalem, crooked with her sins, by tearing her down so that she may be disciplined and repent. God continued destroying Jerusalem by the hand of Babylon, for His stretched-out hand, which is Babylon, does not hesitate until Jerusalem is ruined; therefore the walls and ramparts of Jerusalem became sorrowful over their demolition and the ruin of their city.

2.8.1.en: Her bars: the wide beams in the gates.

2.8.2.en: When Babylon attacked, it broke the gates of Jerusalem and burned them, so they became ashes in the ground and their feet trampled them, and Babylon seized the king and the chiefs of the city, because the people had departed from the law of God; and the prophets became liars who see no visions of God and do not guide the people.

2.9.1.en: He likens Jerusalem to a daughter, that is, a girl, because of her weakness, for the girl is a symbol of bodily weakness. And he says that her elders, that is, the greatest of those in her, sat on the ground in humiliation and lowliness and kept silence, because they had lost the ability to defend her or to give any counsel for escaping the enemies' attack.

2.9.2.en: And because of the dreadfulness of what had befallen them of divine discipline and humiliation, they put dust upon their heads, which is an ancient Eastern custom expressing intense sorrow, and they wear around their waists rough garments, which are sackcloth, also as an expression of sorrow.

2.9.3.en: As for the virgins, who represent hope and joy, humiliation covered them and they bowed their heads toward the ground.

2.10.2.en: My liver is poured upon the earth: my inward parts fell on the ground, an expression that symbolizes the loss of all rest and also symbolizes intense sorrow.

2.10.3.en: The destruction of the daughter of my people: he likens Jerusalem to a weak daughter who has been ground down by the killing of her sons and the humiliation of all who are in her.

2.10.5.en: Jeremiah, of tender feelings, makes clear his intense sorrow in the turmoil of his heart, his continual weeping and his delicate feelings for ruined Jerusalem and the cries of those in her, especially the sight of the children who lose consciousness from hunger as they draw near to death.

2.11.0.en: Their soul is poured out: they die.

2.11.1.en: Jeremiah cannot bear the sight of the children who ask their mothers for food and drink, while the mothers are unable to satisfy their hunger, and they keep asking and crying until they lose consciousness and lean on their mothers' bosoms and then die. They fall from hunger in a swoon like those wounded in war.

2.12.0.en: Equal: I find no city as sorrowful as your sorrow that could be a measure by which the extent of your sorrow is measured, for all sorrows are far less than your sorrow.

2.12.1.en: Before the sorrows of Jerusalem at Babylon's attack upon her, Jeremiah felt that he had lost any ability to warn her, because she had not listened to God's earlier warnings from his mouth, and he cannot caution her because the Babylonian attack has already come upon her; and as for the extent of the ruin she has suffered, he finds no city like her in it, especially since she was the greatest city in the world, for in her was the temple of the Lord. Consequently her sorrow has no measure because of its intensity, and he feels that her ruin is so wide that it has no limits, like the wide sea, so he finds no word with which to comfort her, but is drowned in his sorrow for her sake. It may be that he means that the Babylonian attack is as strong as the raging sea that drowns everything it meets.

2.13.0.en: Causes of banishment: false, misleading information that takes the soul away from God.

2.13.1.en: The prophet makes clear that a basic reason for this ruin is the teaching of the false prophets who spread throughout Jerusalem, so they led the people astray from God and left them to sink into the worship of idols and evil lusts, and gave them a sense of security, so they did not warn them of God's discipline that they might repent. So they remained captives by sin, and they deserved captivity and slavery to Babylon.

2.13.2.en: Do not flatter people with words that take them away from God, but proclaim the truth in the proper way even if some become angry, and take care to encourage them and bear with them even if they wrong you, so that you win their souls for Christ. Do not seek your own comfort but their salvation, and you will gladden the heart of God, who died for your salvation.

2.13.4.en: 15- All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth? 16- All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed her up: certainly this is the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen it. 17- The LORD hath done that which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old: he hath thrown down, and hath not pitied: and he hath caused thine enemy to rejoice over thee, he hath set up the horn of thine adversaries. 18- Their heart cried unto the Lord, O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night: give thyself no rest; let not the apple of thine eye cease. 19- Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.

2.14.1.en: He makes clear the wretchedness to which Jerusalem came after her destruction, to the point that everyone who passes by her mocks her. He sets out a number of expressions of mockery, such as clapping hands and hissing, proclaiming the dreadfulness of her condition, and wagging heads in contempt for her. And they ask how people used to praise her, saying that her beauty was perfect and that she was a joy among all the cities, for her appearance became utterly vile after her ruin.

2.15.0.en: Gnash the teeth: they grind their teeth as a sign of mockery and gloating.

2.15.1.en: From another side, he shows the mockery and gloating of the enemies, harsh upon Jerusalem. They express this by opening their mouths, that is, intense astonishment and contempt, and they hiss and gnash their teeth and rejoice that they have destroyed Jerusalem and that they had longed for this for a long time, that is, the subjection of the whole world to Babylon. So too the neighbors who are jealous of the greatness of Jerusalem gloat over her.

2.16.1.en: Jeremiah affirms that all this destruction is the fulfillment of God's purposes as discipline for His people. He promised from the days of the fathers and of Moses the prophet a reward for the one who obeys His commandments and punishment for the one who breaks them, as He proclaimed the blessings and the curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal (Deut 27:12, 13). So God disciplined His people severely that they might repent, and the strength of the enemies who struck Jerusalem appeared, which is symbolized by the horn, because it is the strongest thing in an animal.

2.17.0.en: Before the mockery and gloating of all against Jerusalem, she finds before her none but God to cry out to, that He may forgive her and remove the punishment from her, and in her remorse she weeps much, so much that he likened the abundance of her tears to a flowing river. He proclaims this sorrow through the ruined wall of Jerusalem, which weeps much; that is, Jerusalem says to God that she has lost all her protection and has no helper but God. And the prophet encourages her to continue weeping and remorse that she may obtain the mercies of God.

2.18.0.en: Watch: a part of the night; the night is divided into three or four watches.

2.18.1.en: The prophet continues encouraging Jerusalem to remorse, that she may offer repentance not only in the daytime but also at night from its beginning, that is, in the first watch, offering repentance with tears and lifting her hands in supplication, especially when she sees her children losing consciousness from so much hunger and almost dying.

2.18.2.en: When tribulation comes upon you, I wish you would not murmur or be troubled over what you have lost, but understand God's purposes and offer repentance, remembering your sins, and be remorseful with tears and prostrations, and make promises of a new life with Him, and you will regain your peace and rest.

2.18.4.en: 20- Behold, O LORD, and consider to whom thou hast done this. Shall the women eat their fruit, and children of a span long? shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord? 21- The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain them in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, and not pitied. 22- Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the LORD's anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.

2.19.0.en: Children of a span long: that is, sucklings.

2.19.1.en: Jerusalem cries out from the intensity of the pain and reminds God that she is His daughter, so why did He humiliate her to this degree? She of course knows that this is divine discipline so that she may repent, but she cannot easily accept this humiliation to which she has come, for from intense hunger the mothers ate their infant children. And the Babylonian violence reached the killing of the elders of the people and its prophets who stood for worship in the temple of God.

2.20.0.en: Jerusalem continues her cry to God, suffering for her young men and her elders, who lie slain and wounded in her streets because of God's severe discipline of her in the day of wrath, that is, by the Babylonian attack upon her.

2.21.1.en: Jerusalem likens the crowd and multitude of the slain and wounded among her sons to their having gathered on a day of feast, one of the feasts of the Lord, but they gathered for sorrow, falling wounded and dead; and those who tried to flee were overtaken by the armies of Babylon, that is, the ruin and killing reached every place and every person. Thus Babylon lost her sons who had been raised and grown up in her, who died by the hand of Babylon, and she was in great fear of her enemies.

2.21.2.en: If you fear God and keep His commandments and keep away from the sources of sin, you become strong and are not troubled by the threats of people, for your God defends you and protects you. So be in constant communion with Him and you will live in assurance. Contrition, hope and repentance: this chapter holds a great place in the rite of the Church, for it is read on one of her most important days, which is Great Friday. It is read at the beginning of the twelfth hour in remembrance of the burial of Christ after His death on the cross; because this chapter is a symbol of Christ, crushed by sufferings for the sake of us sinners. Its words, though they apply to the people of God, Jeremiah writes for the man who speaks; he is crushed and suffers for the sake of his people, a symbol of Christ who suffered and redeemed His people who believe in Him.
